title: PAWS patrol-planning field test removes over 1,000 snares in Srepok Wildlife Sanctuary, Cambodia
summary: PAWS-directed ranger patrols in Srepok Wildlife Sanctuary removed over 1,000 snares in December 2018, versus 200–300 in a typical month.
account: PAWS (Protection Assistant for Wildlife Security) is a machine-learning pipeline that predicts poaching risk and plans patrols. It was field-tested with WWF Cambodia and Ministry of Environment rangers in Srepok Wildlife Sanctuary, Cambodia, from December 2018. Only the month is given, so the first day is used. Rangers received center coordinates of fifteen 3 x 3 km blocks chosen from PAWS risk predictions, without being told each block's risk class. In the first month, 72 rangers in teams of eight detected poaching in 32 cells and removed over one thousand snares. They had reported removing two or three hundred in an average month. Low-risk blocks yielded no poaching. A second trial ran February to March 2019.
purpose: PAWS was built to predict where poaching will occur and to prescribe patrol routes that maximize detection and removal of snares. The snare removals are exactly this intended benefit.
system: PAWS (Protection Assistant for Wildlife Security), enhanced iWare-E predictive model with Gaussian-process uncertainty and game-theoretic patrol planning
model_version: iWare-E with Gaussian-process weak learners trained on January 2015 to April 2018 dry-season data (Xu et al., ICDE 2020)
developer: Harvard University and University of Southern California (Milind Tambe and colleagues), with WWF, WCS and Uganda Wildlife Authority co-authors
deployer: WWF Cambodia with Cambodia Ministry of Environment rangers, Srepok Wildlife Sanctuary

ratings.reason: The ranger force's monthly snare removals rose from a reported two or three hundred to over one thousand. A material gain in patrol effectiveness for the operating team. A chi-squared test confirmed predictions discriminated risk (p = 0.023).

Over one thousand snares were removed from a sanctuary identified as a tiger-reintroduction site. The paper states each snare “represents the life of one animal potentially saved”. A material landscape-scale conservation benefit rather than a documented population-level change.

ai_role.statement: The AI's output (risk-ranked 3 x 3 km blocks) determined where patrols went. Rangers were blinded to risk class. High-risk blocks yielded detections while low-risk blocks yielded none. The paper itself cautions that the first QENP test's increased findings “may be partially explained by factors beyond the predictive model”. The 1,000-versus-200–300 comparison relies on rangers' reported averages, not a controlled baseline. The peer-reviewed paper is written by the system's academic developers together with staff of the operating organizations (WWF, WCS, Uganda Wildlife Authority). There is no commercial vendor.

produced_by: Historical SMART patrol data (2015–2018) sufficient to train a risk model despite 3.6% positive labels
Rangers willing to patrol the suggested blocks and record findings in SMART
Dry-season deployment when rivers are passable and poaching concentrates in the north of the sanctuary
must_hold: Patrol capacity exists to act on predictions (SWS ranger numbers had more than doubled since 2016)
Poacher behavior remains spatially predictable from past detections
Findings are measured against a comparable baseline. The paper notes increases may partly reflect factors beyond the model

echoes.setting: Second SWS trial, February-March 2019: high-risk blocks yielded 7 detections in 22 cells, low-risk blocks 0 in 34 cells (Table III of the same paper)
Ongoing use in Srepok Wildlife Sanctuary; rangers reported finding 5 to 20 times more snares since adopting PAWS, and PAWS was incorporated into SMART

paired_incident.title: Poachers Evaded AI Cameras and Killed Four Rhinos
paired_incident.basis: Same task and domain: AI-directed anti-poaching in a protected area; PAWS patrols removed 1,000 snares, while Ezemvelo KZN Wildlife's AI cameras failed to detect poachers and four rhinos were killed.

headline: PAWS-directed patrols remove over 1,000 snares in Cambodia
metric: removed over 1,000 snares in December 2018, versus 200–300 in a typical month

comparator.against: the rangers' usual monthly snare removal without PAWS
comparator.before: two or three hundred snares in an average month
comparator.after: over one thousand snares in the first month of field tests
comparator.quote: During the first month of field tests in SWS, park rangers detected poaching in 32 cells and removed over one thousand snares—each of which represents the life of one animal potentially saved. The rangers informed us that, by comparison, they typically remove two or three hundred snares in an average month.

later.note: By November 2020 PAWS had been incorporated into the SMART conservation software used in parks worldwide, and Srepok rangers reported finding 5 to 20 times more snares since adopting it.
later.quote: PAWS has been incorporated into the latest update to SMART, which is already used widely by rangers and other park employees to gather data and track observations of illegal activity in parks around the world.
